title: How do you rationalize the cost.
author: count023
selftext:
I was working on a few game prototypes of games i've wanted ot make for years but never had the time, but AI and coding has just made it so much faster that the prototypes are out there now with ease almost exactly the way i dream, but it occured to me that basically after a month or two of work on an incomplete game or prototype, i've spent more in AI subscriptions than buying a game out there already that's close. 

How do you guys all rationalize it? do you expect to publish everything you vibe, is it just a money sink for a personal hobby like airfix models or train sets? stick with purely self hosted stuff tha tonly costs you power you're burning anyway? what?

replies.body: yea, i'd never touch an API for sure, but i did subscribe to max5 tis month for claudeand just can't seem to use it, and in Australia, it's nearly 200AUD per month for that, i suppose that's what hit me hardest when calulatee up the cost of all my subscriptions the last financial year.

comments.author: astrielx
comments.body:
I think if you have to try and convince yourself something is worth it, it probably isn't worth it.

Either you get what you want out of it, or you don't.

replies.author: count023
replies.body: i suppose it's not so much teh "it's not wroth it" was celebrating yesterday a win on getting a project out of a prototype and how much time is aved me, and then i realized that the original game i was basically doing a light remake of, cost only about 50 bucks at the time when it was brand new. and i realized i spent a fair bit more than that recreating it. So it was one of those "huh" type moments.

replies.author: astrielx
replies.body: I mean when you're making it yourself, you can also upgrade and add to the things you like about it rather than waiting for the devs to make any changes (if any) to it. So there's that.

comments.author: DragonfruitDecent862
comments.body:
Hello, old software engineer gone full ai dev here.   Justifying the cost on anything is hard, and if ya have to work fulltime like me, even more so.    Let me give you some information on costs for developers.

For a small studio, costs can range from free to several thousand, and even more. The major reason this is so costly is time. To cut down on time, developers pay for skilled labor, and assets. Digital tools, physical tools like pc hardware, ect. For medium and heavy aaa studios, they are bound by time as well, but mainly efficiency. 

I subscribe to claude max x20. Thats 250 dollars a month, and it has limits, even at that price. 
The major reason i pay so much, is because i understand software, and can leverage ai in my code workflows. In 4 small months, i have made a vulkan game engine with ue5 nanite quality systems, realtime GI, and physics 10 times faster than garrys mod(okay, dont kill me, garrys mod always had slow physics lol). In 4 months i have leverage ai , costing around 1000 bucks, plus a few texture packs on itch.io for textures i can use.   
 Im listing all this to show you what you can do if you understand "how" to leverage it. Most dont, and they burn through money, and have nothing, or little to show for it. Learn what YOU want to do, your end goal. Research how that is "normally" done, and prompt correctly, and in the right steps.

If you want, message me on reddit, and i can point you in the right direction.

replies.author: count023
replies.body:
thanks, i'm an old software engineer myself, been doing it since hte QBASIC days when DOS5.22 was all the rave. I'm not a profesisonal develoepr though, i dabble in scripting and devops for my work as a solution architect ubt i'm mostly sec and gateway engineering, so not super code heavy so most of my usage for AI is purely hobby development, making games i wanted, rverse engineering old games that i wantedt opeek  under the hood at, stuff like that, but it did seem when adding up ai subscriptions over 12 months, ti was quite pricey.

I suppose what really ate into it was that i was bumping up against pro limits and tried max5 this month (and can't even use all that up, the quote outlives me!) and realized that for how much im paying, teh costs far exceeded the amount of money these kinds of games would have been brand new. 

Certainly i use the AI in my work but mostly for stuff that's generally satisfied by my pro subscription, it's onyl the game dev stuff where i was constantly banging against hte weekly limits with gemini and claude that god me thinking afte ri dropped into max5.

replies.author: DragonfruitDecent862
replies.body: Your about as old as me then. Bloody hell im getting old when i remember 56k. I dabbled and had a short run as a community developer for ue4. Me and a few mates worked on the gi system. Laughing on where that is now.. its a please mate. If you need help, just message me. Theres a ......fundamental lack of actual documentation on HOW to use and prompt a llm to do things well. People can go far if they know how software and games work beforehand.      Heres a example.   The aerage vibe coder will start a project like this. "Make me a 3d rts retro game in three.js. top down view. Command and conquer style." This gets the IDEA across, but projects, big long drawn out projects, will become unmanageable.   Instead, try this.  "Start a project. Working name is Mclovens goes to war. Lets make this project a rts game. Model it after command and conquer generals, with a opengl engine. Lets also discuss this before we commit, so we lock down the details without wasting context."  This puts a llm into a foced framework for a scope that is clearly defined, and if you do this on the browser version, make a project that lists what this project is for.  If its claude code or codex, have it make a memory file that loads on startup of your future games rules, and what you have already done, and have not done. That status file is your holy grail.

comments.author: MeasIIDX
comments.body:
Personally, I've never thought about the cost of the subscription in that way. I'm a software engineer and I also record video game music. 

Whenever I purchase new VSTs (virtual instruments and samples), I never think to myself "I wonder if I'll get this value back" because the value has already been provided to me.

I think the same applies to my AI subscriptions which total about $60/month. The value isn't measured by what my output is making me (which is $0) but what it is doing which is a lot compared to the time I've spent writing code manually.

You call it a "money sink" and I feel like if you're already going into it with a mindset that's totally different from mine and that's okay but maybe you need to take a step back and think if this is something you're enjoying or not without the value you're expecting.

comments.author: JustAKoder
comments.body:
The way I’ve rationalized it is through a few different perspectives: 

1. I was pretty anxious about AI taking my job. This is a tangible outlet to release some of that by making sure I’m consistently using the tools AND getting output from them into the world.
2. $200 is a lot of money, but this technology is incredibly powerful. If you can get more proficient at working with it, develop better taste, etc. it is possible to develop something that more than pays for itself (look at OpenClaw).

Idk, I guess I just feel like the expected value is worth it and like I’m doing the right thing to stay up to date and for my skills and don’t worry as much about the payoff timeline.
